amendments.rule: **An anarthrous substantive takes the English the ASV supplies to make it one.** A participle or adjective used as a noun with no article morpheme present still needs an English noun phrase, and the ASV supplies it: a bare *the*, or a pronoun with a relative — *him that*, *them that*, *they that*, *those that*. No article is present to take that English and nothing else licenses it, so it joins the substantive's own unit and is never `added`. `זֵדִים` → *the proud*, `צַדִּיק` → *the righteous*, `יִרְאֵי יְהֵוָה` → *them that feared Jehovah*, `עֹשְׁקֵי` → *those that oppress*, `עֹבֵד` → *him that serveth*. **Head on the word carrying the lexeme**, by rule 31's subtraction: *proud*, *righteous*, *feared*, *oppress*, *serveth*. This does not contradict rule 41's heading on the pronoun. There the supplied pronoun is the whole of what the article is rendered by, so it is the only candidate; here the substantive's own lexeme sits in the same unit and outranks a word the ASV supplied. Read whether an article morpheme is present, and let that decide which rule governs. **And the supplied noun phrase may be built on a generic English noun as readily as on a pronoun.** Where the ASV writes *man*, *men*, *one*, *ones*, *thing*, *things* or another generic noun to make the anarthrous substantive an English noun phrase — `חָכָם` → *the wise man*, `נָבוֹן` → *the man of understanding*, `מַקְשִׁיב` → *man hath regarded* — that noun, together with whatever article, relative or *of* the phrase needs, joins the substantive's own unit on exactly the terms above and is never `added`, and the head stays on the word carrying the lexeme under rules 24 and 31, which already read a substantival adjective's *living creature* as one unit headed on *living*. Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a noun: that ruling governs a noun the ASV supplies where no source nominal stands at all, as `יָשְׁבוּ בָהּ` → *men shall dwell therein* is, and an anarthrous participle or adjective standing in the clause is itself the nominal the English noun phrase is built on. So read whether a source substantive stands for the phrase to realize before marking the noun `added`, exactly as this rule's own first sentence directs for a supplied pronoun. Two riders. Where the Hebrew supplies a relative of its own, that relative takes the *that* and the supplied antecedent goes with it — `לַאֲשֶׁר לֹא עֲבָדוֹ` → *him that serveth him not* puts *him that* on `אֲשֶׁר` — since a present morpheme takes its English before a bare participle does. And where the ASV writes the antecedent once across coordinated substantives, the later ones take only what is written: `וְחֹשְׁבֵי שְׁמוֹ` → *and that thought upon his name* leaves the participle *that thought upon*, under rule 22. **A headless relative clause is read the same way, and its verb may be finite.** Where the Hebrew writes a relative clause with no antecedent noun and no `אֲשֶׁר`, the whole clause stands in a nominal slot and the ASV must supply a noun phrase for it: `אַחֲרֵי לֹא יוֹעִילוּ הָלָכוּ` → *walked after* ***things that do*** *not* ***profit***, `בְלוֹא יוֹעִיל` → *for* ***that which doth*** *not* ***profit***. The supplied antecedent and relative join the clause's own unit and head on the word carrying the lexeme, exactly as *them that* joins a bare participle above and for the same reason: no article and no relative morpheme is present to take them, and nothing else licenses them, so neither is `added`. The unit is discontinuous around the negative or any other intervening word under rule 25, and a Hebrew noun the ASV recasts the same way — `מִבְטַחַיִךְ` → *those in whom thou trustest* — goes with it. **This governs only a clause with no antecedent of its own.** Where the Hebrew writes the antecedent and the ASV supplies a relative for a finite clause juxtaposed to it, nothing in this rule licenses that word: it subordinates a clause rather than making one a noun, and rules 30 and 55 are what decide it. **And a substantive the Hebrew writes is such an antecedent, whatever English this rule supplied to make it one.** An anarthrous participle or adjective for which the ASV has written *him that*, *they that* or *He who* is a written antecedent exactly as a common noun is, so a further relative the ASV writes over a finite clause juxtaposed to it answers to no morpheme and is `added` under rule 55: `נְאֻם שֹׁמֵעַ אִמְרֵי אֵל ... מַחֲזֵה שַׁדַּי יֶחֱזֶה` → *He saith who heareth the words of God ...* ***Who*** *seeth the vision of the Almighty* leaves that *Who* `added`, while the same clause written with a relative of its own — `אֲשֶׁר מַחֲזֵה שַׁדַּי יֶחֱזֶה` → ***Who*** *seeth the vision of the Almighty* — gives the word to the `אֲשֶׁר` under this rule's first rider. Do not read the supplied noun phrase as evidence that what follows is headless: ask whether a substantive stands before the clause, not whether that substantive's own English was written or supplied. Read what the ASV supplied, too, since the headless case writes an antecedent and a relative together — *things that*, *that which* — while a bare relative with no antecedent beside it subordinates a clause to what precedes and is rule 55's. Rule 41's articleless attributive is a third case again, and is decided there. **But those two sentences govern a clause the Hebrew writes, and no more.** Where instead the ASV recasts one Hebrew nominal — the noun together with whatever construct dependents it governs — as an English head noun and a relative clause, and no clause stands in the Hebrew for that relative to subordinate, the relative is part of the noun's own recasting: it joins that noun's unit and is never `added`, exactly as `מִבְטַחַיִךְ` → *those in whom thou trustest* is above. `מִמַּצַּב רַגְלֵי הַכֹּהֲנִים` → *out of the place* ***where*** *the priests' feet stood firm* gives *the place where* to `מַצָּב`, and `אֶל־הַמָּלוֹן` → *unto the place* ***where*** *they lodged* gives the whole phrase to `מָלוֹן`. Head on the word carrying the noun's lexeme under rule 31, which is the English verb where the recasting writes one for it and the head noun where a written Hebrew verb already holds the predicate. **A lexical English verb standing inside such a recasting is not rule 20's supplied lexical verb either**, where that verb is what the noun's own lexeme names — a lodging place is where one lodges and a standing place where one stands — since dropping it leaves that noun's rendering short rather than removing a predication the Hebrew never wrote. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the English relative and ask whether the noun's own rendering is left incomplete, or whether a clause the Hebrew wrote has merely lost a subordinator. Where a Hebrew relative or resumptive morpheme does stand in the phrase it takes the English first, under this rule's first rider and rule 22, and the noun keeps only its own words: `בַּמָּלוֹן אֲשֶׁר תָּלִינוּ בוֹ` → *in the lodging place* ***where*** *ye shall lodge* leaves `מָלוֹן` the bare *lodging place*.
amendments.why: PRO.1 three times has the ASV substantivize an anarthrous adjective or participle with a lexical noun rather than a pronoun: `חָכָם` → *the wise man* and `נָבוֹן` → *the man of understanding* (1.5), and `אֵין מַקְשִׁיב` → *no man hath regarded* (1.24), where `אַיִן` takes the *no* under rule 50 and the participle takes *man hath regarded*. Rule 46's list as it stood reads as pronouns only — *him that*, *them that*, *they that*, *those that* — so a verse pass could take the lexical noun to be unlicensed and mark it `added` under rule 17's supplied-lexical-subject sentence, which would leave the ASV's own noun phrase for a written source substantive unaligned against rule 2. The evidence is already inside the contract rather than new: rule 24 reads a substantival adjective's *living creature* as one unit headed on *living*, and rule 31 governs the whole family of a Hebrew substantive rendered by a multi-word English phrase with a supplied completion, so the generic noun's place in the unit and the head's place on the lexeme are both settled; what was missing was the statement that rule 17's `added` ruling does not reach a noun supplied for a source nominal that is present. The corpus tables for `הַ` show only articular substantivals and contradict nothing here. The amendment widens the list, states the head under rules 24 and 31, and marks rule 17's boundary in rule 17's own terms.

conventions: lo abah rendered 'would none of' (1.25, 1.30): the negative takes the written 'none', and the 'of' goes to whatever governs the object - the written le- at 1.30, and the verb's own valency under rule 44 at 1.25, where the Hebrew writes the object bare and no preposition morpheme stands. 'none of' is not read as one partitive expression under rule 15, since a negative morpheme in the clause is what the 'none' renders, and that count runs before rule 15's supplied-quantifier sentence is reached.

Adjective-plus-noun renderings of a single Hebrew substantive were all decided by rule 31's subtraction and divide two ways in this chapter: the head is the modifier where the English noun is a supplied generic - 'dark sayings' (1.6), 'broad places' (1.20), 'the chief place' (1.21), 'the young man' (1.4) - and the noun where the noun carries the lexeme and the adjective is the ASV's specifier - 'sound counsels' (1.5), 'the careless ease' (1.32). The divergence is the test's outcome and not an inconsistency. 'the young man' is the close one, and the competing head is named in its verse note.

ad matay at 1.22 is split rather than fused, because the ASV writes no separate matrix duration frame there (rule 17's closing sentence): matay takes 'How', carrying the wh-lexeme, and ad takes 'long', carrying the duration. Rule 17's indivisible 'how long will it be' governs only where the ASV writes that frame over a following finite clause.

report: Read all 33 verses end to end against the candidate table. No construction is analysed two ways with nothing in the source to license the difference, so patches is empty.

Supplied preposition reaching a verb's bare object: on the verb at 1.5 (in, unto), 1.12 (into), 1.13 (with), 1.19 (of), 1.22 (in), 1.25 (of), 1.28 (upon); on the written le- at 1.30 (of). The one clause that writes a preposition morpheme is the one where the preposition holds the word - rule 44 against rule 11, not a split. 1.12 and 1.19 are the same participle-in-construct shape and both land the word on the participle, though their notes reach it by different routes (rule 19's carve-out, rule 33's predicate valency).

kol takes an 'of' only where it is itself the nomen rectum (1.17, 1.19) and stands bare where it heads its own chain (1.13, 1.25, 1.30). lo takes 'none' in both 1.25 and 1.30 with the 'of' placed separately; 'none of' is not read as one partitive expression, because a negative morpheme stands in the clause for the 'none'.

The three added units were checked against the whole chapter, since the candidate table is blind to them: 1.5 'That' (protasis with no conjunction morpheme, while the second colon's waw takes 'And that' as one rendering), 1.7 'But' (the verse's one waw stands between 'wisdom' and 'instruction' and holds the 'and' written there), 1.26 'the day of' (head noun and its 'of' both supplied, rule 33's noun-must-be-present limit). Every comparable English word elsewhere in the chapter has a morpheme standing for it.

Rule 31 heads divide by the subtraction test rather than by position: modifier heads at 1.4 'young man', 1.6 'dark sayings', 1.20 'broad places', 1.21 'chief place'; noun heads at 1.5 'sound counsels' and 1.32 'careless ease', where the English noun carries the lexeme and the adjective is the ASV's specifier. Recorded as a convention so a later reader does not read the divergence as a split.

BSB: three disagreements, all documented convention differences and none an error. PRO.1.11 he is MACULA Sh, a paragogic he, unrepresented under rule 32. PRO.1.14 le- and PRO.1.22 la- are silenced by the 'have' recasting (rules 40, 43) and by the ethical dative (rule 40), whose suffix takes the pronoun the ASV writes. No accepted edge was touched for the aggregate.

One promotion, returned as an amendment: rule 46's supplied noun phrase is listed as a bare 'the' or a pronoun with a relative, but this chapter three times has the ASV substantivize an anarthrous adjective or participle with a lexical noun - 'the wise man' (1.5), 'the man of understanding' (1.5), 'no man hath regarded' (1.24). Rule 17's added lexical subject noun sits close enough to be misread, and rule 24 already reads 'living creature' the way this chapter read these, so the amendment widens rule 46's list and names rule 17's boundary.
